title: How Wolves Change Rivers
speaker: National Geographic
description: When wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park, they transformed the entire ecosystem in ways nobody expected.
summary:
In 1995, wolves were reintroduced into Yellowstone National Park after being absent for 70 years. Scientists expected the wolves to reduce deer populations. What they did not expect was that the wolves would change the physical landscape of the park itself.

When wolves arrived, deer began to avoid certain areas — especially valleys and riverbanks where they could be easily caught. This allowed vegetation in those areas to regenerate. Willow, aspen, and other trees grew back along the riverbanks for the first time in decades.

The trees stabilised the riverbanks. This reduced erosion, allowing the rivers to flow in different channels and creating new ponds and wetlands. The entire geography of the rivers began to change.

More trees meant more habitat for beavers, birds, and insects. The recovering ecosystem attracted otters, ducks, and fish. As plant life returned to the valleys, songbird populations increased. Bears returned to eat the berries growing on regenerating bushes.

This process — where the introduction of one species triggers a chain of changes through an ecosystem — is called a trophic cascade. The wolves did not just change the deer population; they changed the rivers, the forests, the wetlands, and ultimately the landscape of Yellowstone.

The story of the Yellowstone wolves is now one of the most famous examples of how predators shape ecosystems. It shows that nature is deeply interconnected — that removing or adding a single species can have consequences far beyond what we initially imagine.

Scientists use the term 'keystone species' for animals that have a disproportionately large effect on their environment. The wolf, it turns out, is one of the most powerful keystone species in North America.

title: What's Hiding at the Most Solitary Place on Earth? The Deep Sea
speaker: Kurzgesagt
description: We have mapped more of Mars than the bottom of our own ocean. What lives in the deep sea is stranger than anything we imagined.
summary:
The deep ocean is the largest living space on Earth — and one of the least explored. Below 200 metres, sunlight disappears entirely. Below 1,000 metres, the ocean becomes completely dark. Yet life exists all the way down to the very deepest point: the Mariana Trench, nearly 11 kilometres below the surface, where pressure is more than 1,000 times that at sea level.

The deep sea is divided into distinct zones. The twilight zone (200–1,000 m) is home to creatures that make daily migrations up toward the surface to feed at night and retreat into the dark during the day. The midnight zone (1,000–4,000 m) is pitch black and near freezing. The abyss (4,000–6,000 m) covers more of Earth's surface than all the continents combined.

Creatures in the deep have evolved extraordinary adaptations. Bioluminescence — the ability to produce light — is the most common form of communication in the ocean. Anglerfish lure prey with a glowing appendage. Vampire squid turn themselves inside-out to reveal bioluminescent patterns. Giant isopods, looking like enormous prehistoric woodlice, scavenge the seafloor.

Hydrothermal vents — cracks in the seafloor where superheated, mineral-rich water erupts — host entire ecosystems that run on chemical energy rather than sunlight. Tube worms metres long, ghostly white crabs, and heat-adapted bacteria thrive in conditions that would kill most life on Earth.

Scientists estimate that fewer than 20 percent of deep-sea species have been discovered. Every expedition returns with creatures never seen before. The deep ocean may also offer clues about how life began on Earth — and whether similar ecosystems might exist in the ice-covered oceans of Jupiter's moon Europa or Saturn's moon Enceladus.

title: Why Elephants Never Forget
speaker: TED-Ed
description: The saying 'an elephant never forgets' is scientifically accurate — and their memories shape the survival of entire herds.
summary:
The saying 'an elephant never forgets' is not just a proverb — it reflects a scientifically documented reality. Elephants possess some of the most impressive long-term memories in the animal kingdom, and these memories play a critical role in the survival of their herds.

Elephants have the largest brains of any land animal, with a highly developed hippocampus — the region associated with memory and spatial awareness. Studies have shown that elephants can remember the locations of water sources they visited decades earlier, recognise the calls and faces of hundreds of individual elephants, and identify specific humans as friendly or dangerous years after a single encounter.

One of the most striking demonstrations of elephant memory involves matriarchs — the oldest females who lead elephant herds. Research in Kenya's Amboseli National Park found that herds led by older matriarchs had significantly higher survival rates, particularly during droughts. When other herd members were uncertain, it was the matriarch's memory of distant water sources and safe migration routes, formed over decades, that guided the group to safety.

Elephants also remember the dead. They have been observed returning to the bones of deceased herd members, touching them carefully with their trunks and feet — behaviour that researchers believe reflects some form of recognition and grief. Elephants mourn, a trait shared with very few other species.

Their memories also serve in social bonding. Elephants recall which individuals have helped or threatened them. This allows them to build complex, long-term relationships across large, fluid social networks — relationships that support cooperative childcare, food sharing, and collective defence.

Elephant memory is not simply remarkable — it is essential. As elephant populations decline due to poaching and habitat loss, the loss of experienced matriarchs removes irreplaceable ecological knowledge that younger elephants cannot replicate.

title: How Volcanoes Work
speaker: National Geographic
description: Volcanoes have shaped Earth's surface for billions of years. Here's the science behind one of nature's most powerful forces.
summary:
Volcanoes are among the most powerful and dramatic forces on Earth. They have shaped continents, influenced climate, and even played a role in the origins of life. But what exactly is a volcano, and how does it work?

Deep beneath Earth's surface, rock becomes so hot that it melts, forming a liquid called magma. Magma is less dense than the solid rock around it, so it rises — slowly pushing through cracks and weak points in Earth's crust. When it reaches the surface, it erupts as lava, ash, or gas. Once magma reaches the surface, it is called lava.

Volcanoes form in several ways. Most are found along the boundaries of tectonic plates — the massive slabs of rock that make up Earth's outer shell and slowly move over millions of years. Where plates pull apart, magma rises to fill the gap. Where plates collide, one plate sinks beneath the other, and the descending rock melts and rises as magma.

Some volcanoes form over 'hot spots' — places where plumes of unusually hot rock rise from deep within the mantle. The Hawaiian Islands were formed this way, as the Pacific plate slowly moved over a hot spot.

Volcanic eruptions vary enormously. Some produce gentle flows of lava that move slowly down hillsides. Others are explosive, hurling ash and rock fragments kilometres into the atmosphere. The largest eruptions in Earth's history released enough material to alter the global climate for years.

Despite their destructive power, volcanoes are also creative forces. Volcanic soil is extremely fertile, which is why people have farmed near volcanoes for thousands of years. Volcanic activity also releases gases that, over billions of years, helped form Earth's atmosphere and oceans.

title: Is the Amazon Rainforest Disappearing?
speaker: TED-Ed
description: The Amazon is home to 10% of all species on Earth and regulates rainfall across a continent — and it is being destroyed faster than ever.
summary:
The Amazon rainforest is the largest tropical forest on Earth, stretching across nine South American countries and covering over 5.5 million square kilometres. It is home to roughly 10 percent of all species on the planet — an estimated 40,000 plant species, 1,300 bird species, and 3,000 freshwater fish. No ecosystem on Earth contains a greater concentration of biodiversity.

The Amazon also plays a critical role in regulating the global climate. Its trees absorb vast quantities of carbon dioxide, storing carbon that would otherwise contribute to global warming. But the Amazon's climate role goes further: through a process called transpiration, trees release enormous amounts of water vapour, which forms clouds and generates rainfall — not just over the Amazon itself, but across South America and beyond. The Amazon, in a very real sense, makes its own weather.

Yet the Amazon is disappearing. Since the 1970s, over 20 percent of the forest has been cleared — an area larger than France. The primary drivers are cattle ranching, soy farming, illegal logging, and road construction. Deforestation typically follows roads: once a road cuts into the forest, settlers, farmers, and ranchers follow.

Scientists are increasingly concerned about a 'tipping point.' The Amazon generates rainfall partly through its own trees. As deforestation reduces tree cover, rainfall decreases — causing more trees to die in a reinforcing cycle. Beyond a certain threshold, large parts of the Amazon could shift permanently from rainforest to dry savanna, releasing enormous quantities of stored carbon in the process.

Indigenous communities, who have lived in the Amazon for thousands of years, are among the most effective protectors of the forest. Deforestation rates are consistently lower in indigenous territories than in other areas — a fact increasingly recognised by governments and conservation organisations.

title: How Climate Change Affects Us All
speaker: National Geographic
description: Climate change is already affecting communities around the world. Here's what the science says — and what it means for the future.
summary:
Climate change is no longer a distant future threat. Its effects are already being felt around the world — in rising sea levels, more intense storms, prolonged droughts, and shifting seasons. Understanding what is happening and why is essential to making informed decisions about how to respond.

The Earth's climate has always changed. Over millions of years, the planet has experienced ice ages, warm periods, and dramatic shifts driven by changes in Earth's orbit, volcanic activity, and other natural factors. What is different now is the speed of change — and the cause.

Since the Industrial Revolution, human activities have released enormous quantities of greenhouse gases — primarily carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels — into the atmosphere. These gases trap heat from the sun that would otherwise escape into space. As their concentration rises, more heat is retained, and global average temperatures increase. The planet has already warmed approximately 1.1 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.

The effects are wide-ranging. Glaciers and ice sheets are melting, contributing to sea level rise that threatens coastal cities and low-lying nations. Warming oceans are more acidic and less oxygen-rich, harming marine life. Extreme weather events — heatwaves, floods, wildfires, hurricanes — are becoming more frequent and intense.

The communities most affected are often those least responsible for causing climate change. Small island nations face complete inundation. Subsistence farmers in Africa and Asia face worsening droughts. Arctic communities see the landscapes they have lived on for generations literally disappearing.

The scientific consensus is clear: limiting warming to 1.5 or 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels requires rapidly reducing greenhouse gas emissions and transitioning away from fossil fuels. The decisions made in the coming years will shape the climate for centuries.

title: The Science of Sleep
speaker: National Geographic
description: Sleep is not just rest — it is one of the most active and essential processes your brain and body perform.
summary:
We spend about a third of our lives asleep. For most of human history, sleep was considered a passive state — a simple shutdown of the body and mind. Modern science has revealed a very different picture. Sleep is an active and essential biological process, during which some of the most important work of the brain and body takes place.

Sleep occurs in cycles of about 90 minutes, each containing different stages. During slow-wave sleep, the body does much of its physical repair work — releasing growth hormone, repairing tissues, and strengthening the immune system. During REM sleep — characterised by rapid eye movement and vivid dreams — the brain is highly active, consolidating memories and processing emotional experiences.

Memory and learning are strongly linked to sleep. Studies show that people who sleep after learning new information remember it significantly better than those who stay awake. The sleeping brain replays and strengthens memories, moving information from short-term to long-term storage. This is why 'sleeping on a problem' often results in new insights in the morning.

Lack of sleep has serious consequences. After just one night of poor sleep, reaction times slow, concentration falls, and emotional regulation deteriorates. Chronic sleep deprivation is linked to increased risk of obesity, heart disease, diabetes, and mental health problems. People who regularly sleep less than seven hours a night have significantly higher rates of illness.

Despite this, modern life consistently works against good sleep. Artificial light — particularly the blue light from screens — suppresses the production of melatonin, the hormone that signals sleep. Work schedules, social pressures, and digital technology keep people awake longer than their biology recommends.

Scientists increasingly view sleep not as a luxury but as a biological necessity — as essential to health as food and exercise.

title: How Do Satellites Get & Stay in Orbit?
speaker: SciShow Space
description: There are thousands of satellites orbiting Earth right now — but how do they get there, and what keeps them from falling back down?
summary:
Right now, thousands of satellites are orbiting Earth — providing GPS navigation, weather forecasting, internet connectivity, and scientific data. But how do they get into orbit, and what keeps them from falling back to Earth?

The key to understanding orbits lies in a simple but counterintuitive idea: a satellite in orbit is constantly falling. Gravity pulls it toward Earth just as it pulls everything else. But the satellite is also moving sideways so fast that as it falls, the Earth curves away beneath it at the same rate. The result is a continuous freefall that never reaches the ground. This is what an orbit is.

To get a satellite into orbit, a rocket must accelerate it to orbital velocity — roughly 7.9 kilometres per second (about 28,000 km/h) for low Earth orbit. At that speed, the satellite's forward momentum exactly balances Earth's gravitational pull. Go faster, and the orbit rises. Go slower, and the satellite spirals back down.

Different missions require different orbits. Low Earth Orbit (LEO), between about 160 and 2,000 kilometres altitude, is used for the International Space Station, many Earth observation satellites, and the Hubble Space Telescope. Medium Earth Orbit (MEO), around 20,000 kilometres, is where GPS satellites operate. Geostationary Orbit (GEO), at exactly 35,786 kilometres, is where communications and weather satellites sit — at this altitude, a satellite takes exactly 24 hours to complete one orbit, so it appears stationary above a fixed point on Earth.

Satellites do face some drag, especially in lower orbits where trace amounts of atmosphere still exist. Without occasional boosts from onboard thrusters, they would slowly lose altitude and burn up on re-entry. Managing satellite orbits — including safely deorbiting old satellites to reduce space debris — is a growing challenge as the number of satellites continues to increase.
